headline_marked: [[Backboard CLI outscores Claude Code and Codex]] on Terminal-Bench with 85.4% via Claude Opus 4.8
headline: Backboard CLI outscores Claude Code and Codex on Terminal-Bench with 85.4% via Claude Opus 4.8
summary: A Canadian startup's coding agent achieved an 85.4% score, surpassing top entries from Anthropic and OpenAI on the challenging Terminal-Bench 2.1 leaderboard.
details: Backboard CLI achieved an 85.4%   0.8% score on Terminal-Bench 2.1, with a pass@5 of 0.888, utilizing Claude Opus 4.8 via Bedrock. This score places it above published entries from Claude Code with Fable 5 (83.8%) and Codex with GPT-5.5 (83.1%), developed by Anthropic and OpenAI respectively.

Backboard, a startup from Nepean, Ontario, developed this coding agent. The achievement highlights that frontier-level agentic coding performance can be reached by smaller teams without billion-dollar compute resources.

Terminal-Bench is a rigorous benchmark featuring 89 real terminal tasks, designed to simulate complex, multi-step developer workflows. The leaderboard is typically dominated by major AI labs using their proprietary models and agents.

The team emphasizes that the "harness"   how an agent plans, delegates, and manages context   is as crucial as the underlying model. This approach allowed their agent to maximize the capabilities of an external model.

The benchmarking process was transparent and rigorous: five sequential jobs, identical configuration, all 89 tasks, and five attempts each (445 trials total). All trials were included, with errored attempts counting as zero, and logs made public.
Backboard plans to open source the CLI soon, believing that developer adoption and feedback are key to its success. The tool is model-agnostic, providing flexibility to users.
The CLI is currently available at backboard.io/cli. The team encourages developers to try it out and provide feedback, which directly reaches the builders.

headline_marked: [[Fake Wi-Fi network set up on Delta flight]] by suspected DEF CON attendees, FBI investigating
headline: Fake Wi-Fi network set up on Delta flight by suspected DEF CON attendees, FBI investigating
summary: Passengers on a Delta flight from Las Vegas to Atlanta allegedly created a fake Wi-Fi hotspot to harvest credentials, prompting an FBI investigation.
details: The FBI Atlanta office is investigating an incident where passengers on a Delta flight allegedly spoofed the onboard Wi-Fi. No arrests have been made in connection with the incident so far.

The event occurred on Monday on Delta flight 591 from Las Vegas to Atlanta, just one day after the DEF CON security conference concluded. Social media accounts tracking air-to-ground messages first reported the anomaly.

Pilots reportedly sent a message stating passengers from a cyber conference 'were able to jam our WiFi and broadcast their signal.' A Reddit description claimed a fake hotspot, 'Delta WiFi Fast,' was created with a phishing page to collect credentials.

This technique, known as an 'evil twin' attack, involves setting up a rogue Wi-Fi network to intercept login information and other sensitive data. It is a well-known method within the IT security community.
Delta confirmed an 'unauthorized WiFi network' was present briefly but stated the flight's safety was never compromised. No aircraft operating systems were affected, and no emergency was declared.

The FBI Atlanta bureau confirmed it is in contact with local and corporate partners regarding the potential Wi-Fi incident. Officials noted that no arrests were made, and agents did not meet the flight upon arrival.
